Subject:    City of Berkeley Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Project CEQA
            Hydrology and Water Quality Memo




The City of Berkeley is seeking authorization to redevelop the City’s Solid Waste and Recycling
Transfer Station (SW&RTS, proposed project) located on a 7.73-acre site at the intersection of
Gilman Street and Second Street in the northwest corner of the City (see Figure 1). The existing
Transfer Station was constructed in 1983 with the sole purpose of receiving the City’s solid
waste. Over the course of the next fifteen years the facility was expanded to include other
services related to waste handling, recycling, and disposal (Zero Waste, 2019). The proposed
design, outlined in the Solid Waste and Recycling Center Transfer Station Feasibility Study Final
Report (‘Feasibility Study’) prepared by Zero Waste Collaborative in 2019, will provide the City
of Berkeley with an integrated facility that can accept a variety of materials and ensure
environmentally compliant methods will be implemented for the handling and processing of
refuse, fiber and container recyclables, and compostable materials not only for today but for
many decades to follow (Zero Waste, 2019).

The objectives of this report are to outline the existing regulatory hydrologic framework that
governs the development of the project site, identify the potential impacts of the project on
environmental quality as it pertains to hydrology and water quality, and address potential
methods to mitigate any identified impacts to a less than significant level. It is our understanding
that this report will be incorporated with other CEQA permitting documentation; therefore, we
have formatted it in a consistent manner.

1.1           REGULATORY SETTING
This section describes the federal, state, and local regulatory context to be considered for the
proposed project, and addresses hydrology and water quality concerns, including development
strategies, stormwater pollution prevention plans, and stormwater management practices.




220104 Balance Hydrologics CEQA_Memo_082322         2
                                                                          BALANCE HYDROLOGICS, Inc.


1.1.1    Federal and State Regulations
             1.1.1.1     Section 402 of the Clean Water Act
The Clean Water Act (CWA) authorizes the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to regulate
water quality in California by controlling the discharge of pollutants to water bodies from point
and non-point sources through the National Pollution Discharge Elimination System (NPDES).

In Alameda County, as with the rest of the Bay Area, NPDES permits are administered by the
San Francisco Bay Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB), a division of the State
Water Resources Control Board (SWRCB). Phase I of the NPDES program covered discharges
from industrial sites, construction sites larger than five acres, and municipal separate storm sewer
systems (MS4s) serving populations of more than 100,000 people. The Phase II expansion of the
MS4 program in 1999 expanded its coverage to include “Small” MS4s that serve:

•        Urbanized areas as defined by the U.S. Census;

•        Areas of high growth or high growth potential;

•        Areas that discharge to sensitive water bodies or another regulated MS4; and,

•        Areas that make a significant contribution to pollution of waters of the U.S.

Stormwater discharges in the City of Berkeley, as with all of Alameda County, are permitted
under the NPDES requirements for large MS4s (Phase I). The SWRCB has established a
Municipal Regional Stormwater permit (Regional Municipal Permit) for the Bay Area Counties
(and permittees with the Counties) of Alameda, Contra Costa, Santa Clara, and San Mateo, along
with the Fairfield-Suisun and Vallejo permitees (Order No. R2-2015-0049, NPDES General
Permit No. CAS612008) to regulate stormwater discharges in these areas. All eligible MS4s are
required to comply with its provisions, which include construction- and post-construction-phase
stormwater runoff controls and water quality best management practices (BMPs) for new and re-
development.

MS4 owners/operators must reduce pollutants in storm water to the maximum extent practicable
(MEP) to protect water quality. The regulations specify that compliance with the MEP
requirement can be attained by developing a storm water management plan that addresses the six
minimum control measures described in the storm water regulations (Berkeley, 2016).

The Regional Municipal Permit provisions include post-construction provisions to prevent non-
storm water discharges, minimize the discharge of pollutants in storm water runoff, and prevent a
development-caused worsening of stream channel erosion and sediment deposition resulting
from hydromodification of a watershed. To minimize pollutant discharges, projects must provide
the capacity to either infiltrate, evapotranspire, or otherwise treat all runoff generated by the 85th
percentile storm event. 1 Typically this is completed using low impact development (LID) design


1
 The 85th percentile storm represents a specific intensity for which all storms of lesser or equal intensity generate
85 percent of the total annual rainfall, while more intense storms only generate 15 percent of the total.


220104 Balance Hydrologics CEQA_Memo_082322                3
                                                                       BALANCE HYDROLOGICS, Inc.


principles that seek to minimize the amount of land covered by impervious surfaces and
maximize opportunities for infiltration. In instances where this cannot be completed solely using
LID features, treatment measures must be provided to remove or otherwise neutralize identified
pollutants. High flow rates that cannot be sufficiently reduced by site design strategies must be
controlled through the provision of detention storage or through stabilization of downstream
conveyances that would be adversely affected by development. Because these treatment and
detention facilities will require maintenance for the life of a development project, developers
must also establish a dedicated funding responsibility for either the future owners of the land or a
designated public entity. In its role as an MS4 operator and permit holder, Alameda County is
required to enforce these site design and water quality protection measures for all new and
redevelopment projects within its jurisdiction. The City of Berkeley participates in the Alameda
Countywide Clean Water Program, which is a joint effort with the other municipalities in the
County to prevent stormwater pollution, protect and enhance water quality in creeks and
wetlands, preserve beneficial uses of local waterways, and comply with State and Federal
regulations.

Construction Sites
The SWRCB administers the NPDES General Permit for Discharges of Stormwater Runoff
Associated with Construction Activity (General Construction Permit). In order to cover a
construction project disturbing one acre or more of land under the General Construction Permit,
a facility must submit a Notice of Intent to the SWRCB prior to the beginning of construction.
Effective July 1, 2010, all dischargers are required to obtain coverage under the Construction
General Permit Order 2009-0009-DWQ adopted on September 2, 2009. The General
Construction Permit requires that projects develop and implement a Stormwater Pollution
Prevention Plan (SWPPP), identifying potential sources of pollution and specifying runoff
controls during construction for the purpose of minimizing the discharge of pollutants in
stormwater from the construction area. The SWPPP should contain a site map which shows the
construction site perimeter, existing and proposed buildings, lots, roadways, storm water
collection and discharge points, general topography both before and after construction, and
drainage patterns across the project (see Figure 2 in Appendix A). The SWPPP must list BMPs
the discharger will use to protect storm water runoff and the placement of those BMPs.
Additionally, the SWPPP must contain a visual monitoring program, a chemical monitoring
program for "non-visible" pollutants to be implemented if there is a failure of BMPs, and a
sediment monitoring plan if the site discharges directly to a water body listed on the 303(d) list
for sediment.

The permit also includes post-construction standards with the requirement for all construction
sites to match pre-project hydrology to ensure that the physical and biological integrity of aquatic
ecosystems is maintained. This “runoff reduction” approach is analogous in principle to LID and
serves to protect related watersheds and water bodies from both hydrologic-based and pollution
impacts associated with the post-construction landscape.




Consequently, treatment facilities designed to accommodate runoff from the 85th percentile storm have sufficient
capacity to treat 85 percent of total annual runoff.

            1.1.1.1       Section 401 of the Clean Water Act
Under the auspices of the CWA, the United States Army Corps of Engineers (USACE)
administers permitting programs that authorize impacts to "waters of the United States"
including "wetlands" and "other waters." Such impacts may not be permitted until the SWRCB,
acting through its regional boards, certifies that the activities covered by the permit will not
violate water quality standards. Certification must be consistent with the requirements of the
federal CWA, CEQA and California Endangered Species Act, and with the SWRCB's mandate
to protect beneficial uses of waters of the state.

The San Francisco Bay RWQCB has adopted the USACE policy that there shall be "no net loss"
of wetlands. Thus, prior to waiving or certifying water quality, the RWQCB requires a proposed
project to ensure there are no impacts on existing wetlands, or, if such impacts are unavoidable,
that they are fully mitigated.

             1.1.1.2     California Porter-Cologne Act
The Porter-Cologne Act requires "any person discharging waste, or proposing to discharge
waste, within any region that could affect the waters of the State (any surface water or
groundwater, including saline waters) to file a report of discharge" with the local RWQCB by
applying for waste discharge. The RWQCB determines if a project should be regulated pursuant
to this act based on the likelihood that it would pose any "threat" to water quality. The San
Francisco Bay RWQCB considers the placement of clean fill in waters of the State to constitute
"pollution," because it can potentially alter existing water quality, which may adversely affect its
beneficial uses.

Areas that drain to the San Francisco Bay are regulated by the Region 2 (San Francisco Bay)
Basin Plan which was approved in 1995 and most recently updated in 2019. Beneficial water
uses are designated in the Basin Plan for local aquifers, streams, marshes, and rivers, as well as
water-quality objectives that must be met to protect these uses. Identified beneficial uses for
Codornices Creek include cold- and warm- freshwater habitat, fish migration, preservation of
rare and endangered species, fish spawning and wildlife habitat, and contact and non-contact
recreational uses. In addition, the Basin Plan establishes water quality management objectives for
various contaminants and pollutants (CA RWQCB, 2019).

             1.1.1.3     California Fish and Game Code
Existing stream channels in California are protected under sections 1600-1603 of the State Fish
and Game Code. These regulations specify that it is a landowner's responsibility to obtain a state
permit before undertaking any modifications within an existing stream channel up to the top of
bank. Stream channels are defined by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) as
exhibiting evidence of scour, having a definable bank, or having or being capable of supporting
riparian vegetation.

             1.1.1.4     Sustainable Groundwater Management Act
In 2014, a new law was signed intended to create a framework for sustainable management of
groundwater resources in California. The law, called the Sustainable Groundwater Management


220104 Balance Hydrologics CEQA_Memo_082322        5
                                                           BALANCE HYDROLOGICS, Inc.


Act (SGMA), requires governments and water agencies with management responsivities in
medium- and high-priority subbasins to halt groundwater overdraft through development of a
Groundwater Sustainability Plan (GSP). East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) and the
City of Hayward have submitted a Draft Groundwater Sustainability Plan for the East Bay Plain
groundwater subbasin, which includes the area underlying the City of Berkeley (Luhdorff &
Scalmanini, 2021). The Draft GSP establishes the sustainability goals, measurable objectives,
minimum thresholds, and potential undesirable results if the goals of the GSP are not met.
Projects and management actions geared toward achieving the sustainability goals are also
included in the report.

1.1.2    Local Regulations
             1.1.2.1     Alameda County Storm Water Program
As noted above, the operators of municipal storm sewer systems must comply with the
permitting provisions of the NPDES. The Alameda County Clean Water Program (ACCWP) is a
joint effort of Alameda County, the cities of Alameda, Albany, Berkeley, Dublin, Emeryville,
Fremont, Hayward, Livermore, Newark, Oakland, Piedmont, Pleasanton, San Leandro, Union
city, the Alameda County Flood Control and Water Conservation District (ACFCD), and the
Zone 7 Water Agency for managing conditions of the NPDES permit and addressing potential
stormwater quality concerns. Though the entities of the ACCWP carry out their own individual
stormwater pollution prevention programs, the ACCWP provides for the coordination and
consistency of approaches between the individual participants and documents their efforts in
annual reports.

ACCWP has developed several resources as guidance for projects toward various requirements
of the NPDES permit. Of key importance are the documents outlining requirements and practices
for new development within the county (ACCWP, 2021), which include construction-phase
BMPs and technical guidance for post-construction runoff management. An important aspect of
the post-construction runoff management outlined by the ACCWP is hydromodification
management; the technical guidance states that all new projects must mitigate peak flows from
10 percent of the 2-year rainfall event up to the 10-year event to protect downstream waterways
from degradation. To facilitate compliance with the hydromodification standard, the guidance
encourages the use of the Bay Area Hydrology Model (BAHM), a continuous simulation
modeling software created by Clear Creek Solutions to help applicants size specialized detention
facilities (ACCWP, 2021).

             1.1.2.2     Alameda County Flood Control District
Current practice and standards associated with flood control for Alameda County are outlined in
the Alameda County Flood Control and Water Conservation District’s (ACFCD) Hydrology and
Hydraulics Manual. The manual stipulates peak flow design requirements for stormwater holding
facilities to mitigate downstream flooding associated with the increase in impervious area of new
and re-development. As it pertains to this project, ACFCD guidance stipulates that post-




220104 Balance Hydrologics CEQA_Memo_082322     6
                                                                     BALANCE HYDROLOGICS, Inc.


development peak runoff must not exceed the pre-development peak runoff for the 5-, 15-, 25-,
and 100-year recurrence interval storm events 2 (ACFCD, 2018).

             1.1.2.3     City of Berkeley Department of Planning and Development
Additional standards related to hydrology and water quality management are included in the City
of Berkeley General Plan (General Plan), published by the Department of Planning and
Development in 2003. Within the General Plan, two main sections – referred to in the text as
elements - highlight the City’s current policy regarding hydrology and water quality. The two
elements are Environmental Management and Disaster Preparedness and Safety.

1.1.2.3.a Environmental Management Element

Within the Environmental Management Element of the General Plan, the City outlines five
policies – EM-23 through 27 - that are designed to improve water quality within City creeks and
the San Francisco Bay. While some of the points emphasize adherence to existing legislation,
they also expand upon state and county level regulations. For example, policies stipulate a need
to eliminate sanitary and storm sewer cross connections; establish 30-foot setbacks from open
and culverted creeks; 3 and improve community awareness of water quality management.

1.1.2.3.b Disaster Safety and Preparedness Element

Under the sub-heading Flood Hazards within the Disaster Safety and Preparedness Element, the
General Plan outlines three policies – S-26 through 28 – that define measures to address flood
hazards within the City. In summation, the element seeks to reduce the threat from existing flood
hazards, prevent additional flood hazards from future development, and make flood insurance
costs less prohibitive for property owners in the City.

1.2           ENVIRONMENTAL SETTING
1.2.1    Regional Hydrology
Codornices Creek, which collects runoff from roughly 10% of the City of Berkeley’s area, is
present along the northern boundary of the project site (Figure 2). This creek is notable within
the region for several reasons. Primarily, it is one of the least culverted creeks in the East Bay
and as a result, supports a substantial salmonid population (Hagar, 2005). Furthermore, the creek
has seen multiple restoration efforts in the past twenty years that have focused on improving the
section of creek between San Pablo Avenue and the Union Pacific Railroad (UPRR), just
upstream of the project site. Downstream of the project site and Second Street, the creek is
culverted under I-80 before it discharges into the Bay north of Golden Gate Fields (see Section
1.2.3 for a discussion of the I-80 culvert and localized flooding).

The Gilman Street subwatershed (‘Gilman Basin’) is located to the south of the project site. The
Gilman Basin is the second smallest watershed in the city, servicing roughly 249 acres of heavily

urbanized area within the lower Bay Plain area of the City of Berkeley. The basin is entirely
culverted and outfalls into the Bay at the western end of Gilman Street (Balance, 2011).

Average annual rainfall in the Codornices Creek and Gilman Basin watersheds are
approximately 24 and 20 inches, respectively; higher rainfall amounts fall on the Berkeley Hills
where the Codornices Creek watershed originates, as opposed to the low-lying western portion of
the city that the Gilman Basin services. Nearly 95 percent of this precipitation falls during the
winter rainy season, October through April, with the heaviest rainfall typically occurring in
December, January, and February.

sorting/storage area. The remaining portion of the project site (just over 6 acres) drains to the
culverted Gilman Basin. This south-draining areas includes the main transfer station with a

1.2.3     Downstream Hydrology
Runoff from the site that drains to the Gilman Basin is collected on Second Street and conveyed
by pipe a quarter mile to the system’s outfall at the western end of Gilman Street. This
infrastructure downstream of the project site is undersized for the 10-year peak flow event
(Balance, 2011). Under current conditions, flows exceeding the 10-year event will back-up
within the storm drain system and cause ponding on surface streets and other low-lying areas.
Due to the Gilman Basin’s low time-of-concentration for stormwater runoff (a result of the small
size and high imperviousness of the watershed) flooding is most prominent during short-
duration, very high intensity rainfall events.

To the north of the project, Codornices Creek is culverted below I-80 prior to discharging into
the Bay. The I-80 culvert has been the subject of significant study given that it constricts flow in
the Creek, inducing flooding on Second Street adjacent to the project site. 5 Flooding has been
further exacerbated since the conveyance of the UPRR culvert was increased when it was
replaced in 1999 (Klein, 2009); a larger culvert upstream allows for more water to pass under the

1.2.4    Project soils and groundwater
Near surface soils underlying the project site are classified as urban fill and clay loam, both of
which have a low infiltration capacity (SoilWeb, 2021). More broadly, the project site is in a
region dominated by alluvial fans – ranging in depth from 100 to 200 feet below ground surface
(bgs) - deposited on a west-sloping bedrock surface (Groundwater Committee, 1999). Due to the
proximity to the Bay, groundwater levels at the project site range seasonally from 5 to 10 feet
bgs (Luhdorff and Scalmanini, 2021). Given the history of industrial work in this part of
Berkeley, there are multiple active contamination cleanup programs within a half-mile of the
project site, the most notable being an actively managed hexavalent chromium plume associated
with the WRE/Colortech Facility located on 6th Street. Further contaminants of concern include
petroleum by-products, tetrachloroethylene, lead, and other heavy metals (Geotracker, 2021).

1.3           PROJECT IMPACTS
1.3.1    Thresholds of Significance
Appendix G to the CEQA Guidelines includes questions for determining whether impacts to
hydrology and water quality are significant. These questions reflect the input of planning and
environmental professionals at the Governor’s Office of Planning and Research and the
California Natural Resources Agency, based on input from stakeholder groups and experts in
various other governmental agencies, nonprofits, and leading environmental consulting firms.
They also reflect the regulatory requirements of laws other than CEQA that protect hydrology
and water quality (e.g., the federal Clean Water Act, the Porter-Cologne Water Quality Control
Act). As a result, many lead agencies derive their significance criteria from the questions posed
in Appendix G. The City has chosen to do this for this project.

Accordingly, the impact of the proposed project on hydrology and water quality would be
considered significant if it would:

      (a) violate any water quality standards or waste discharge requirements or otherwise
          substantially degrade surface or groundwater quality;
      (b) substantially decrease groundwater supplies or interfere substantially with groundwater
          recharge such that the project may impede sustainable groundwater management of the
          basin;
      (c) substantially alter the existing drainage pattern of the site or area, including through the
          alteration of the course of a stream or river or through the addition of impervious
          surfaces, in a manner that would:

             (i) result in substantial erosion or siltation on- or off-site

             (ii) substantially increase the rate or amount of surface runoff in a manner that would
                  result in flooding on or off-site;



220104 Balance Hydrologics CEQA_Memo_082322         11
                                                               BALANCE HYDROLOGICS, Inc.


             (iii) create or contribute runoff water that would exceed the capacity of existing or
                  planned stormwater drainage systems, or provide substantial additional sources of
                  polluted runoff; or

             (iv) impede or redirect flood flows

    (d) in flood hazard, tsunami, or seiche zones, risk release of pollutants due to project
        inundation;

    (e) conflict with or obstruct implementation of a water quality control plan or sustainable
        groundwater management plan.

1.3.2    Water Quality Standards, Surface, and Groundwater Quality
Stormwater contaminants from the site may be present in the runoff that is discharged from both
the construction and post-construction phase of the proposed project. The potential for site runoff
to affect water quality and/or hydromodification is evaluated below.

             1.3.2.1     Surface Water Quality
Construction Phase
During construction, clearing, grading and other activities would increase the potential for on-
site erosion, potentially leading to increased turbidity and sedimentation in Codornices Creek
and the Gilman storm drain. Sedimentation in Codornices Creek may degrade in-stream habitat
and reduce flow capacity at downstream culverts and open channels, potentially inducing or
exacerbating flooding. Other pollutants that might impact surface water quality during project
construction include petroleum products (gasoline, diesel, kerosene, oil, and grease),
contaminants from construction debris, hydrocarbons from asphalt paving, paints, solvents, and
litter.

Because the project would disturb more than one acre of land, the applicant is required to prepare
a SWPPP, per NPDES general construction permit requirements through the SWRCB. The
SWPPP would address potential erosion and sedimentation issues through a project-specific
erosion control plan, as well as other BMPs to reduce the potential for increased off-site
sedimentation, spills, and other contamination from on-site construction activities. Appropriate
measures for control of sediment and other pollutants from construction sites are included in the
“Construction Handbook of Best Management Practices” (CASQA, 2019). The project SWPPP
is likely to include, but is not limited to, the following BMPs related to construction water-
quality impacts:

         •   If the entire site is not graded in a single operation, leave existing vegetated areas
             undisturbed until construction of improvements on each portion of the development
             site is ready to begin;

         •   Immediately re-vegetate or otherwise protect all disturbed areas from both wind and
             water erosion upon completion of grading;


220104 Balance Hydrologics CEQA_Memo_082322        12
                                                               BALANCE HYDROLOGICS, Inc.


         •   Collect storm water runoff into stable drainage channels and/or small drainage basins
             to prevent the buildup of large, potentially erosive storm water flows;

         •   Direct runoff away from all areas disturbed by construction;

         •   Use sediment ponds or siltation basins to trap eroded soils before runoff is discharged
             into on-site or off-site drainage culverts and channels;

         •   Install straw rolls, hay bales or other approved materials below all disturbed areas
             adjacent to drainages and drainage inlets to prevent eroded soils from entering the
             stream channel. Maintain these control measures until all disturbed upslope areas are
             fully stabilized;

         •   To the extent possible, schedule major site development work involving excavation
             and earthmoving for construction during the dry season;

         •   Develop and implement a program for the handling, storage, use, and disposal of
             fuels and hazardous materials. The program shall also include a contingency plan
             covering accidental hazardous material spills;

         •   Avoid cleaning, fueling, or maintaining vehicles on-site, except in an area designated
             to contain and treat runoff; and

         •   After construction is completed, inspect all drainage facilities immediately
             downstream of the grading site for accumulated sediment, and clear these facilities of
             debris and sediment as necessary.

In addition, the project site has the potential to experience stormwater run-on during large storm
events when the capacity of the adjacent Codornices Creek channel is exceeded. The project
SWPPP will need to include provisions to account for these flows during construction. Potential
items not included in the list above may include:

         •   Staging work on the northern end of the project site (the area adjacent to Codornices
             Creek) early in the project so that the new flood protection berm is in place while the
             remainder of the construction proceeds.

         • Phasing and scheduling the project to complete demolition and major earthwork
           during the dry season when run-on would not occur.

         •   Use of temporary retaining walls or other methods to reduce the risk of run-on to the
             project site during the construction period.

In compliance with the requirements of the statewide NPDES Construction General Permit, the
developer will prepare a SWPPP for submittal with a Notice of Intent to the RWQCB prior to the
start of construction. The SWPPP would specify BMPs to be employed during the construction
phase to control sediment loads and pollutants. The SWPPP shall include the minimum BMPs
required for the identified Risk Level of the project and receiving waters. BMP implementation
shall be consistent with the BMP requirements in the most recent version of the California


220104 Balance Hydrologics CEQA_Memo_082322       13
                                                                       BALANCE HYDROLOGICS, Inc.


Stormwater Quality Association Stormwater Best Management Handbook-Construction or the
Caltrans Stormwater Quality Handbook Construction Site BMPs Manual. Proper implementation
of the project-specific SWPPP would reduce the potential construction-related water quality
impacts to a less-than-significant level. No further mitigation is required.

Operational Phase
Based on two preliminary design concepts that include a vegetated set-back from Codornices
Creek and a focus on landscaped area throughout the site, the proposed project would decrease
the site’s total impervious percentage from 98 to approximately 89 percent. 6 Despite this
decrease in impervious surface, it is possible that more runoff to the storm drain system will be
generated on-site. Currently, waste material sorting and temporary storage is done in uncovered
areas and runoff that falls on these areas is diverted to holding tanks prior to being sent to an
EBMUD sanitary sewer line under special permit. 7 With the implementation of the proposed
design, rainfall will no longer be able to interact with waste material as all material handling will
be done in covered areas. One result of this water quality improvement, assuming that special
discharge is no longer required, is that a larger portion of runoff will be generated within the
Gilman Basin watershed. While runoff from the newly roofed areas is no longer expected to
contact waste debris, it may still contain pollutants typical of urban area impervious surfaces. As
required by the NPDES permit, runoff from these areas (and all other impervious surfaces on the
project site) will still require appropriately designed stormwater quality treatment measures. As
described in the Feasibility Study, stormwater BMPs are expected to include media filter
treatment vaults, and rainwater harvesting and re-use cisterns, as methods of treating or
preventing stormwater runoff from impervious surfaces (Zero Waste, 2019). With the
implementation of the proposed suite of stormwater BMPs, the potential for the project to have
an operational phase impact on stormwater quality is less than significant.

Codornices Creek Watershed
Regarding the northern portion of the site that drains to Codornices Creek, the proposed design
calls for a vegetated set-back from the creek that will replace a portion of the existing natural gas
fueling station and container storage area. The remainder of the area will serve as the entryway
for the main public scale 8 (Zero Waste, 2019). All stormwater discharge from impervious
surfaces in this area will be treated in facilities to comply with ACCWP water quality treatment
requirements. Facilities will be incorporated into landscaped areas surrounding the proposed
buildings, parking areas, roads, and related impervious infrastructure. Proper design, sizing, and
implementation of treatment measures, as outlined in ACCWP’s C.3 Stormwater Technical
Guidance, will effectively address both water quality and hydromodification concerns; because
the Codornices Creek watershed is a zone of special consideration, as defined by the ACCWP in
Section 7.2 of the C.3. Guidance, it is subject to hydromodification requirements. Given that the

proposed project will include the addition of a vegetated, landscaped buffer along Codornices

conditions, stormwater runoff that drains to Codornices Creek will likely improve under post-
project conditions; therefore, the impact related to stormwater quality will be less than
significant.

Gilman Basin
As stated above, by moving all the waste sorting and recycling processes indoors there will be a
net increase in runoff from the project site to the Gilman Basin. To ensure that the increase in
runoff does not impair water quality downstream of the project, LID and treatment vaults
employed onsite will be designed to meet water quality standards outlined by the ACCWP’s C.3.
Stormwater Technical Guidance. Because water is conveyed solely by pipe downstream of the
project site in the Gilman Basin, the portion of the project located in Gilman Basin is not located
in an area susceptible to hydromodification as defined in Section 7.2 of the CCCWP C.3.
Guidance (ACCWP, 2021).

Through the adherence to design standards outlined above and the implementation of a
stormwater control plan, in compliance with the Regional Municipal NPDES Permit, stormwater
quality and hydromodification impacts will be reduced to a less-than-significant level in both
watersheds. No mitigation is required.

             1.3.2.2     Groundwater Quality
The stormwater treatment BMPs discussed above are likely to be constructed as media filter
treatment vaults, given the relatively shallow groundwater conditions at the project site. The
BMPs are expected to meet water quality treatment standards as required under Provision C.3 of
the Regional Municipal NPDES Permit.

Even if final designs incorporate vegetated swales or flow-through planters as stormwater
treatment measures, underdrains 9 would be required, given the low soil infiltration rates and high
groundwater conditions. In addition, with a known plume of groundwater contamination in the
vicinity of the site, the use of underdrains for these features is preferred to avoid the potential
increased mobilization of the existing plume. Mitigation Measure HYD-1 requires that any
proposed stormwater treatment features included as part of the final design incorporate
underdrains to reduce potential impacts to groundwater quality to a less-than-significant level.

1.3.3    Groundwater supplies and recharge
Water supply for the proposed project is obtained from EBMUD. The proposed project would
not pump groundwater at the project site or otherwise use groundwater for supply, and therefore
would not deplete local groundwater supplies.

9
  An underdrain consists of one or multiple small diameter perforated pipes installed at the bottom of a stormwater
treatment BMP. In situations where infiltration into the underlying soil is either not feasible or not wanted, it
conveys the treated runoff from the BMP filter media to downstream stormwater drainage infrastructure.

The existing site surface area is currently 98% impervious. The proposed project would decrease
the overall imperviousness to approximately 89% by creating a vegetated set-back from
Codornices Creek and implementing landscape-based LID design features. Due to the proximity
of the project to the Bay, and the high groundwater table (see Section 1.2.4), there is no major
opportunity for the use of infiltration when selecting these features or stormwater treatment
BMPs. Furthermore, given the existing groundwater contamination mentioned above, measures
will likely be implemented to avoid significant groundwater recharge – see Mitigation Measure
HYD-1. As a result, the potential impact to groundwater recharge is considered less than
significant.

1.3.4    Altered Drainage Patterns
             1.3.4.1     Erosion or Siltation On- or Off-Site
Construction-phase impacts relating to erosion or siltation both on and off-site are discussed in
Section 1.1.2.1, above. Implementation of the project specific SWPPP in compliance with
County regulations would reduce erosion and siltation during project construction. The resulting
impact would be less than significant.

Compliance with the NPDES Phase II Permit through the ACCWP, and the addition of a
vegetated set-back to the portion of the site that drains to Codornices Creek, will limit post-
construction hydromodification effects that could induce in-stream erosion and cause siltation in
Codornices Creek. As the Gilman Basin storm drain is a direct, piped outfall to the Bay, there is
no concern for hydromodification. 10 As such, the impact related to potential hydromodification
effects would be less than significant.

             1.3.4.2     Flooding On- or Off-Site
The proposed project would decrease the overall imperviousness of the project site surface area
from 98 percent to approximately 89 percent, primarily through the incorporation of a vegetated
set-back from Codornices Creek and through implementation of landscape-based LID design
features. In general, this decrease would be expected to slightly reduce the overall runoff from
the project site relative to existing conditions, especially for the Codornices watershed where the
majority of the imperviousness will be removed. Despite the decrease in imperviousness, the
additional stormwater runoff from newly covered areas (water that was diverted to EBMUD
under existing conditions, see Section 1.2.2.1) has the potential to cause or exacerbate flooding
downstream of the project site. This would represent a potentially significant impact.

Preliminary hydrologic modeling was completed by Balance Hydrologics using the project
description and site concepts outlined in the Feasibility Study to determine how the change in
land use and stormwater conveyance covered in Section 1.2.2 would affect stormwater runoff
from the project site. The modeling was performed using USACE’s HEC-HMS modeling
program and reflects the methodology outlined in ACFCD’s guidance explained in Section
1.1.2.2. For the purposes of this analysis, the project site was modeled as a single drainage area.

  Per Chapter 7 of the Alameda County C.3 Technical Guidance Manual (ACCWP, 2017), hydromodification

and because flooding is of particular concern in this area, especially for the Codornices

watershed, Mitigation Measure HYD-2 is included to confirm that final project designs and

to HYD-2, potential impacts related to increase in stormwater flows would be reduced to a less-
than-significant level.

             1.3.4.3     Exceedance of Storm Drain Capacity
Both the Codornices and Gilman Street watersheds have stormwater capacity constraints
downstream of the project site for flows with a 10-year or greater recurrence (see Section 1.2.3).
As discussed in the previous section, stormwater runoff from the site is expected to decrease
under post-project conditions. Detailed stormwater routing has not yet been designed for post-
project conditions, though the site drainage is expected to remain generally the same. Per
discussion with ZWD staff, the final design of either Concept A or B are not anticipated to result
in the rerouting of current drainage patterns but if portions of the project site that previously
drained to one watershed are diverted to the other, exceedance of storm drain capacity may occur
despite the overall decrease in stormwater runoff. To address this potentially significant impact,
Mitigation Measure HYD-3 provides guidance for final design of the stormwater infrastructure.
Compliance with Mitigation Measure HYD-3 would confirm that the project does not
exacerbate storm drain capacity constraints and would reduce the potential impact to a less-than-
significant level.

             1.3.4.4     Hydrologic Impacts to Flood Flows
During significant storm events the highest likelihood of flooding in Codornices Creek occurs
adjacent to and on the northern portion of the project site where Second Street acts as a point of
release for the creek (see Section 1.2.2). The capacity of the culvert beneath I-80 lacks the
necessary conveyance for events equal to or greater than the 10-year recurrence interval. This
currently results in flooding adjacent to and on the project site at Second Street. Because the
proposed project includes a setback in compliance with the City of Berkeley Creek Ordinance
that will be graded at or below the existing site grade, the overbank storage volume will be
improved compared to existing conditions. For the purposes of impacts to flood flows, CEQA
directs lead agencies to evaluate whether a proposed project would cause or risk exacerbating
existing flooding conditions by bringing development or people into an affected area. Because
the proposed project would improve the existing flooding conditions on the project site and
within Second Street, impacts to flood flows would be less than significant.

While the City does not identify a threshold requiring evaluation of climate change on flooding
and CEQA does not require analysis of the existing environment’s effect on future users or
residents of a project unless the project itself exacerbates an existing risk or hazard, this provides
a discussion of potential flooding impacts related to climate change for informational purposes.
The additional vegetated buffer along the southern boundary of Codornices Creek would provide
minor additional storage that is unlikely to reduce the breakout of flood flows to Second Street;
however, the setback does provide space for a future response to climate change when the
incorporation of future adaptive measures is feasible and necessary. For example, a flood wall
could be constructed as sea level rise further exacerbates existing flooding conditions.

1.3.5    Risk of Pollutant Release Due to Inundation
Due to the proximity of the project site to San Francisco Bay, it is subject to potential inundation
by tsunami. 12 Maps provided by the California Geological Survey (CGS) 13 show the potential
tsunami inundation zone extending from San Francisco Bay to 5th Street, east of the project site.
The proposed project would replace existing infrastructure, but the overall elevation and usage of
the site would generally remain the same. The proposed project would not cause the site to be
more susceptible to tsunami inundation, and thus the risk of resultant pollutant release would be
less than significant when compared to existing conditions.

Federal Emergency Management Agency maps for the Berkeley/Albany area show the presence
of Special Flood Hazard Area (Zone AO; the 1-percent chance annual flood or what has
traditionally been called the ‘100-year flood’ hazard zone) for Codornices Creek adjacent to the
northern boundary of the project site. The project site itself is within the 0.2-percent annual
chance Flood Hazard Area (‘500-year flood’) that covers the East Bay Plain in this area between
Highway 80 and 4th Street. Though rare, the current site is subject to potential flooding from the
adjacent Codornices Creek, which would (if water quality treatment storage capacity is
exceeded) result in release pollutants to downstream receiving waters. However, the proposed
project (under both Concept A and Concept B) would include a 30-foot creek buffer and berm
wall that would serve to reduce the risk of run-on flooding relative to existing conditions. As
such, the potential impact related to release of pollutants due to flood inundation is less than
significant.

1.3.6 Water Quality Control Plan and Sustainable Groundwater Management Plan
Consistency
As discussed in Sections 1.1.1.2 and 1.1.1.4, the proposed project falls within the jurisdiction of
the San Francisco Bay Water Quality Control Plan (CA RWQCB, 2019) and East Bay Plan
Groundwater Management Plan (EBMUD and Hayward, 2021). In both cases, the proposed
project would continue existing uses on a similar footprint to existing conditions and would not
have significant impacts related to water quality or groundwater (see Sections 1.3.2 and 1.3.3).
Proposed stormwater BMPs would be designed to meet NPDES standards and are consistent
with the goals and objectives outlined in the Basin Plan. In some cases, project plans have
specifically targeted ways to reduce the potential for generation of contaminated runoff
(e.g., covering areas designated for material handling and sorting).

With respect to the Groundwater Management Plan, the project site is located in a heavily
urbanized area of the East Bay Plain, with a long-standing history of light and heavy industrial
uses. Because of these previous and existing industrial land uses, the underlying aquifer is not a
regional source of water supply, nor is it anticipated to be developed as one in the future. The
project would not intensify use at the site, nor would it significantly affect groundwater recharge
to, or movement within, the underlying aquifer relative to existing conditions.

1.4           CUMULATIVE IMPACTS
The cumulative context to assess the project impacts include the current and historic land use of
the project site and the broader region of Berkeley; the potential hydromodification impact to
Codornices Creek; and the potential to worsen existing flooding near the project site. When
analyzing cumulative impacts, the watershed is used as the geographic unit based on the concept
that many water quality problems, like the accumulation of pollutants or nonpoint source
pollution, are best addressed at the watershed level. In addition, California’s regulatory
framework for protection of water quality focuses on the watershed. Potential cumulative
impacts specific to water quality, flooding, and groundwater are discussed below.

1.4.1    Surface Water Quality
The Codornices and Gilman watersheds are both highly urbanized and include past and existing
heavy industrial facilities within the lower portions near the project site. In addition, much of the
development in this area originally occurred prior to the passage of the Clean Water Act, and,
though many sites have been re-developed and/or retrofitted since, legacy water quality impacts
remain. Because of the high existing level of urbanization within these watersheds (especially the
Gilman Street watershed), future development is likely to consist largely of infill and
redevelopment projects and, similar to the proposed project, will be required to incorporate
updated stormwater quality treatment measures in compliance with applicable federal, State, and
local laws and regulations. With respect to cumulative surface water quality impacts,
implementation of cumulative projects would not contribute to a considerable cumulative impact.

Due to the small percentage of the project site that falls within the Codornices Creek watershed
and the planned setback from the creek, the proposed project would likely not have a large
impact on the overall water quality of the watershed if treatment requirements are met.
Conversely, in the Gilman Basin, there is potential for the project to improve water quality by
incorporating additional and updated stormwater treatment measures (compared to existing
conditions) that comply with current NPDES treatment requirements and all other applicable
federal, State, and local laws and regulations. The existing facility had to retroactively implement
requirements to meet standards after the passage of major environmental legislation listed in
Section 1.1.1 and has struggled with upholding the requirements outlined for industrial
facilities. 14 By designing the proposed facility to meet necessary treatment requirements, the
potential for pollutants to enter receiving waters would be greatly reduced. Therefore, the
proposed project would not make a cumulatively considerable contribution to the less than
significant cumulative impact and the cumulative impact would be less than significant.




14
  In April of 2016 the non-profit organization San Francisco Baykeeper filed a complaint against the City of
Berkeley alleging that the existing facility was violating its Industrial Stormwater Permit regulated under Section
402 of the Clean Water Act.

1.4.2    Flooding
Both watersheds currently lack sufficient capacity to handle storm events larger than the 10-year
event and face an existing impact from flooding. Codornices Creek is constrained by the culvert
under I-80 and insufficient overbank storage between the UPRR and I-80 that results in overland
release to Second Street. In the Gilman Basin, the storm drain system is undersized such that
storm flows back up and flood low-lying areas along Gilman Street at events greater than a 10-
year recurrence. Future cumulative development and redevelopment along Codornices Creek
would continue to add additional overbank storage near the creek in compliance with the City of
Berkeley Creek Ordinance. Given the existing high level of urbanization within both watersheds,
large-scale cumulative flooding impacts are unlikely, especially when considering the increased
emphasis on LID design and the opportunities to retrofit detention facilities. With respect to
cumulative flooding impacts, implementation of cumulative projects would not contribute to a
considerable cumulative impact.

The proposed project would reduce stormwater runoff to both watersheds (see Section 1.3.4.2)
and would provide additional overbank storage along Codornices Creek (see Section 1.3.4.4).
Therefore, the proposed project would not make a cumulatively considerable contribution to the
less than significant cumulative impact and the cumulative impact would be considered less than
significant.

1.4.3    Groundwater
Based on the high degree of urbanization in West Berkeley and the generally low-infiltration
soils in the area, there is minimal recharge to the underlying groundwater and most rainfall is
conveyed as surface runoff to San Francisco Bay. Future projects in the area would be required
to incorporate LID elements in accordance with applicable federal, State, and local laws, which
encourage infiltration, where subsurface conditions allow. With respect to cumulative impacts to
groundwater recharge, implementation of cumulative projects would not contribute to a
considerable cumulative impact.

The proposed project would decrease impervious area by approximately 9 percent. As discussed
in Section 1.3.3, because of the proximity of the project site to the Bay, and the high
groundwater table, there is no major opportunity for the use of infiltration when selecting LID
design features or stormwater treatment BMPs. However, this is an existing condition, and the
proposed project is not expected to cumulatively decrease groundwater recharge below existing
conditions. Therefore, the proposed project would not make a cumulatively considerable
contribution to the less than significant cumulative impact and the cumulative impact would be
considered less than significant.

Groundwater quality within the West Berkeley area has been significantly impacted by past
industrial activities. Redevelopment within this area, especially conversion of heavy industrial
uses to lighter industrial, commercial, or residential uses, would likely result in general
improvements in water quality under future cumulative conditions. With respect to cumulative
impacts to groundwater quality, implementation of cumulative projects would not contribute to a
considerable cumulative impact.



220104 Balance Hydrologics CEQA_Memo_082322    21
                                                              BALANCE HYDROLOGICS, Inc.


The project itself would maintain a similar land use to existing conditions and is not expected to
degrade groundwater quality (see Section 1.3.2.2). Therefore, the proposed project would not
make a cumulatively considerable contribution to the less than significant cumulative impact and
the cumulative impact would be considered less than significant.

1.5           MITIGATION MEASURES
Impact HYD-1: The proposed project could potentially mobilize existing contaminant plumes
located near the project site if infiltration-based LID measures are used to treat stormwater runoff
in compliance with NPDES requirements.

Mitigation Measure HYD-1: Infiltration will not be used in LID elements to avoid the
possibility of mobilizing existing contaminant plumes. LID features will be fitted with
underdrains that collect and convey treated stormwater to the existing storm drain infrastructure
located on Second Street.

Impact HYD-2: The proposed project could potentially alter the existing drainage pattern of the
site or area in a manner that would significantly increase the rate or amount of surface runoff
resulting in flooding off-site.

Mitigation Measure HYD-2: In compliance with ACFCD requirements, prior to approval of the
final project design by the City of Berkeley, the project proponent shall complete a hydrologic
study to show that, at a minimum, peak flow from the project site does not increase for the 5-,
15-, 25-, and 100-year storm events. If appropriate detention capacity cannot be provided to meet
this requirement, then the site design shall be altered to reduce impervious area (or otherwise
alter the drainage), such that the flood control requirements can be met.

Impact HYD-3: Per discussions with ZWD staff the proposed project is not anticipated to alter
existing drainage patterns, however, the proposed project has the potential to alter site drainage,
shifting drainage from one sub-watershed to another. This could exacerbate existing storm drain
capacity issues even if the overall peak runoff from the site is reduced. This would be a
significant impact related to storm drain capacity.

Mitigation Measure HYD-3: Prior to approval of the final project design by the City of
Berkeley, the project proponent shall provide documentation that the final stormwater plan
maintains the existing proportion of runoff between the Codornices and Gilman Street
watersheds, or that peak flows are not increased in each subwatershed for the 5-, 15-, 25-, and
100-year storm events. If increases in peak flow are documented at that time, the project shall
provide additional detention or plans shall be altered to re-apportion flows such that no peak-
flow increases shall occur to either watershed.

               STORMWATER POLLUTION PREVENTION PLAN
              City of Berkeley Transfer Station and Recycling Center
                    1201 Second Street and 669 Gilman Street
                                Berkeley, California


A.     INTRODUCTION

This document is the Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) for the City of Berkeley
(City) Transfer Station and Recycling Center located at 1201 Second Street and 669 Gilman
Street, Berkeley, California, respectively. The Recycling Center is owned by the City but
operated by the Community Conservation Center (CCC). The SWPPP was prepared in
accordance with the requirements of the California State Water Resources Control Board (State
Board), National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) General Permit for
Stormwater Discharges Associated with Industrial Activities dated April 1, 2014, as amended by
Order WQ 2015-0122-DWQ and Order WQ 2018-0028-DWQ (General Permit).

This SWPPP sets forth specific practices, procedures, monitoring, and reporting that are the
responsibility of designated Facility personnel to implement.

A.1    PLAN OBJECTIVES

This SWPPP is designed to:

          Identify and evaluate sources of pollutants associated with industrial activities that
           may affect the quality of stormwater discharges and authorized non-stormwater
           discharges (NSWDs) from the Facility;
          Identify and describe the minimum Best Management Practices (BMPs) (General
           Permit Section X.H.1) and any advanced BMPs (Section X.H.2) implemented to
           reduce or prevent pollutants in industrial stormwater discharges and authorized
           NSWDs; and
          Identify and describe conditions or circumstances which may require future
           revisions to this SWPPP.

The SWPPP provides Facility staff with guidance for achieving the stated objectives and
maintaining compliance with the requirements of the General Permit. A copy of this SWPPP is
maintained at the Facility.

                                                                                                    1
A.2      REGULATORY BACKGROUND

The United States Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA) developed the stormwater
regulatory program through the authority of the Clean Water Act amendments of 1987. The
U.S. EPA’s goal was to reduce discharges of contaminated stormwater from industrial facilities.
The U.S. EPA, through the NPDES permitting program, regulates discharges of potentially
contaminated wastewater and stormwater into Waters of the United States. California has been
delegated NPDES general permitting authority by the U.S. EPA. On April 1, 2014, the State
Water Resources Control Board (SWRCB) adopted Order 2014-0057-DWQ. This General Permit
became effective on July 1, 2015. The General Permit was subsequently amended by Order WQ
2015-0122-DWQ and Order WQ 2018-0028-DWQ. This SWPPP was written pursuant to the
requirements set forth in the General Permit.

A.3      EXISTING FACILITY PLANS AND PLAN COMPLIANCE MODIFICATIONS (GENERAL PERMIT
         SECTION X.D.2)
This section lists permits and other governing documents that may be relevant to water
quality-related issues. In addition to the General Permit, the following documents have been
taken into account while preparing this SWPPP:
      1. 303(d)-list of impaired water bodies;
      2. Total maximum daily loads (TMDLs);
Additional documents that may affect practices employed to control stormwater discharges
associated with industrial activities include the following:
      3. Spill prevention control and countermeasures plan, which describes petroleum storage,
         handling, and spill response activities at the Facility (updated 10 November 2021); and
      4. Hazardous material business plan, which maintains an inventory of hazardous
         chemicals, hazardous materials storage volumes, and hazardous materials storage
         locations (updated 2019).

This SWPPP will be amended and revised as needed. SWPPP revisions will be completed when:

            BMPs require significant changes;
            There is a physical or operational change at the Facility which may affect
             stormwater discharges;
            Otherwise deemed necessary by the Pollution Prevention Team members based on
             visual observations (General Permit XI.A.3);
            Upon entering Level 1 or Level 2 status (General Permit XII.1.C);
                                                                                               2
          Additional pollutant source is identified;
          Modification is made to the Monitoring Implementation Plan (MIP);
          Change is needed to prevent Numeric Action Level (NAL) exceedances;
          Annual Comprehensive Facility Compliance Evaluation (ACFCE) identifies necessary
           changes;
          Modifications required to be consistent with applicable municipal, state, and federal
           requirements pertaining to the General Permit;
          Directed to do so by the Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB); and
          There are changes to alternative discharge location identification (General Permit
           XI.C.3.b), Representative Sampling Reduction justifications (General Permit XI.C.4.c),
           or Qualified Combined Samples justification (General Permit XI.C.5.c).

Significant SWPPP Revisions are required to be certified and submitted via SMARTS within 30
days of the significant revision. Other revisions (other than typographical errors) are required
to be submitted within three (3) months. The pollution prevention team will assess what is
significant. If no changes are made to the SWPPP, there are no resubmittal requirements. A
revision sheet has been provided to track revisions made within this SWPPP.

Per Section XV of the General permit, the Discharger shall revise the SWPPP, as appropriate,
and implement the revisions within 90 days of the ACFCE.

A.4    PLAN AVAILABILITY AND RECORDS RETENTION (GENERAL PERMIT SECTION XXI.J AND
       SECTION XXI.H)

Paper or electronic records of documents required by this SWPPP will be retained for a
minimum of five (5) years from the date generated or date submitted, whichever is later, for
the following items:

          Employee Training Records;
          BMP Implementation Records;
          Spill and Clean-up Related Records;
          Records of Monitoring Information;
          Records of Visual Observations;
          Response to the observations including identification of SWPPP revisions, if needed;
          Level 1 Exceedance Response Action (ERA) Reports;

                                                                                                   3
          Level 2 ERA Action Plan;
          Level 2 ERA Technical Report; and
          Annual Reports from SMARTS (checklist and any explanations).

Upon request by the relevant agency, the Facility will provide information to determine
compliance with this General Permit to the SWRCB, RWQCB, U.S. EPA, or local Municipal
Separate Storm Sewer System (MS4) within a reasonable amount of time. The Facility will
furnish, upon request by the relevant agency, copies of records that are required to be kept by
this General Permit. In addition, the electronic version of the SWPPP will be uploaded to
SMARTS.

A.5    PERMIT REGISTRATION DOCUMENTS & SIGNED CERTIFICATION (GENERAL PERMIT
       SECTION II.A)

Permit Registration Documents (PRDs) are to be submitted through the Stormwater Multiple
Application and Report Tracking System (SMARTS) by the Legally Responsible Person (LRP), or
authorized personnel (i.e., Duly Authorized Representative) under the direction of the LRP.
PRDs include:

   1. Notice of Intent (NOI);
   2. Signed Certification Statement (LRP Certification is provided electronically with SMARTS
      PRD submittal);
   3. Site Map(s);
   4. SWPPP; and
   5. Annual Fee.
The individual designated as the LRP and other authorized personnel are identified in
Section B. SMARTS submittal documentation, including a copy of NOI and Signed Certification
Statement, is attached in PRDs, Appendix A of this SWPPP. The Facility Site Maps are included
as Figures 1 through 4.

A.6    TEMPORARY SUSPENSION OF ACTIVITIES (GENERAL PERMIT SECTION X.H.3)

The General Permit includes a provision for facilities that temporarily suspend industrial
activities for ten (10) or more consecutive calendar days during a reporting year. In the event
the Facility’s operations are temporarily suspended, the SWPPP will be revised to include
stabilization BMPs. In addition, the date the Facility is fully stabilized and projected start date

                                                                                                      4
will be documented. If monitoring is infeasible, justification for not monitoring will be
provided. The revised SWPPP will be uploaded via SMARTS within seven calendar days prior to
suspension of activities.

B.     POLLUTION PREVENTION TEAM (GENERAL PERMIT SECTION X.D.1)

The LRP, DAR, and Pollution Prevention Team designated for this Facility are summarized
below. In the event a regularly assigned Pollution Prevention Team member is temporarily
unavailable, a new member will be assigned the role by the LRP or DAR. Team members are
cross-trained to assist with various activities, as necessary, to implement this SWPPP in the
event staff become unavailable due to vacation, illness, or other reasons.

The procedures to identify alternate team members to implement the SWPPP and conduct
required monitoring when the regularly assigned team members are temporarily unavailable
are listed below.

Transfer Station, Ecology Center and CCC SWPPP BMP staff are all trained. In the event one
person is not available, other trained staff are available to perform the duties. Only trained staff
implement the SWPPP.

Monitoring, sampling, reporting and General Permit administrative tasks are contracted out to
consulting firms. These consulting firms have personnel that are available to implement the
General Permit for the City.

The Facility training program is detailed in Section H of this SWPPP.

C.2    FACILITY DESCRIPTION

The facility consists of two operations: the Transfer Station in the northern and central portion
and the Recycling Center in the southern portion of the site.

The Transfer Station encompasses 5.0 acres and is operated by the City of Berkeley. Facilities
on this portion of the site include the Administration Building, Transfer Station/Tipping Floor,
Equipment Maintenance Building, Used Oil Depot, Scale House, Temporary Mobile Diesel
Fueling Tank, Wash Rack, Container Maintenance Building, Container/Bin Storage Areas,
General Storage Area, Green Waste Receiving Area, General/Electronic Waste Storage, and
Parking.

The Transfer Station is owned and operated by the City to accept municipal, commercial and
private solid waste and transfer it to a sanitary landfill. The Transfer Station does not accept
hazardous waste or infectious materials. It accepts scrap metals, construction debris,
refrigerated appliances, electronic waste, mattresses and box springs, used tires, propane
cylinders, and green waste.




                                                                                                                  7
Equipment is fueled on site with a mobile diesel fueling tank. Equipment is repaired on site in
either the Equipment Maintenance Building or the Container Maintenance Building.
Equipment, vehicles, and refuse bins are cleaned at the wash rack.

The Recycling Center borders the Transfer Station to the south and encompasses 2.4 acres.
This portion of the site includes the CCC and Ecology offices, parking, Paper and Glass
Recycling Warehouses, Glass Sorting Area, Commingled Container Storage, Universal Waste
Storage, Customer Recyclable Area, Recyclable Buyback Area, Ecology Administrative Shed,
and Parking.

The Recycling Center is owned by the City and currently operated by the CCC. The Recycling
Center accepts recyclable materials from the pickup of recyclables by the Ecology Center and
from the general public. Minor equipment maintenance is performed on site and fueling takes
place at the Transfer Station by the mobile diesel fueling tank.

C.3     SITE STORMWATER DRAINAGE
The site is located in the Gilman Street watershed, which is a highly urban and industrial
section of the City. Site drainage is conveyed through the City storm drain system (south on
2nd Street and west on Gilman Street) and drains into the San Francisco Bay at the Gilman
Street outfall.

The site encompasses 7.4 acres of land that slopes towards the Bay. Approximately 98 percent
of the site is paved with asphalt or concrete, buildings or other structural facilities.

The facility includes 11 Drainage areas (Drainage Areas 1 through 11) of which one is non-
industrial (Drainage Area 11). Drainage Areas 1-11 are depicted on Figure 3. A description of
the Drainage Areas is provided below.

Drainage Area 1

This Drainage Area contains Container Bin Storage, and a Container Maintenance Building
which also stores tires. Additionally, garbage trucks and heavy equipment are temporarily
stored in this area while awaiting scheduled maintenance.

Stormwater in this area flows to two trench drains and a catch basin CB-1 then is directed to a
Contech filter for treatment, after which it is discharged into the City’s stormwater conveyance

                                                                                                  8
system in Second Street. Stormwater samples are collected from the Contech filter's discharge
point, at DP-1A.

Drainage Area 10 may overflow into Drainage Area 1 during large storm events that exceed
the available storage capacity (21,000-gallon or 42,000-gallon storage volume when an extra
aboveground storage tank [AST] is brought on site). Additionally, while no off-site run-on from
Codornices Creek has been observed entering Drainage Area 1, Second Street may flood with
municipal stormwater during large storm events at the end of the cul-de-sac. When flooding
occurs, it may impede the flow within the storm drain lines in Drainage Area 1 resulting in on-
site pooled water.

Drainage Area 2

This Drainage Area contains the Scale House, a portion of the Equipment Maintenance
Building, General Waste Storage, Truck Parking, Mattress Area, the Wash Rack which drains to
the East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) under permit, vehicle/customer access areas, a
portion of the non-industrial Employee Parking Area, and a non-industrial Administration
Building.

Stormwater in Drainage Area 2 flows to two trench drains (TD-2 and TD-2A) and a catch basin
(CB-2) (Figure 3). Stormwater from TD-2 flows to an underground conveyance system and to
the Contech filter. Stormwater from TD-2A and CB-2 flows to a manhole and then to a Contech
filter. Stormwater from catch basin and trench drains passes through the Contech filter and is
sampled at the effluent side of the vault (DP-2A).

Drainage Area 3

This Drainage Area contains a portion of General Waste Storage, General Storage, Temporary
Mobile Diesel Fueling, a portion of the Equipment Maintenance Building, Used Oil Depot, and
Drum/Diesel Exhaust Fuel Storage.

Stormwater flows through a strip drain depression on the north side of the Equipment
Maintenance Building and is directed to catch basin CB-3A which flows to CB-3. CB-3 also
receives overland flow from the area north of the Wash Rack. Stormwater on the eastern
portion of the Drainage Area flows to catch basin CB-4 which flows to a manhole and then


                                                                                                  9
connects to underground piping to a Contech filter. Stormwater from CB-3 and CB-4 passes
through the Contech filter and is sampled at the effluent side of the vault (DP-3A).

Drainage Area 4

This Drainage Area contains industrial areas including Truck Parking, and a portion of the
Container Bin Storage Area, and non-industrial areas including a portion of the Administration
Building and a portion of the Employee Parking area.

Sheet flow leaves the facility along the western portion of this Drainage Area. Therefore, a
Representative Sampling Reduction (RSR) sampling point, DP-4 was designated as described in
Section M.3. Stormwater that discharges from Drainage Area 4 flows into the City's stormwater
conveyance system on Second Street (see Figure 3).

Drainage Area 5

This Drainage Area contains The Ecology Center’s office, Storage Shed, Truck Parking, and
maintenance. Portions of this area are bermed which directs sheet flow to leave the facility
along the western portion of this Drainage Area. Therefore, a RSR sampling point, DP-5A has
been designated as described in Section M.3. Stormwater that discharges Drainage Area 5
flows into the City's stormwater conveyance system on Second Street (see Figure 3).

Drainage Area 6

This Drainage Area contains Recycling Bins, Customer Recyclable Area, Universal Waste and
Fats Oil and Grease Storage. Materials are unloaded and placed within canopy covered bins.
Water in this drainage area flows northwest towards Second Street. Sheet flow leaves the
facility along the western portion of this Drainage Area. Therefore, a RSR sampling point, DP-6
has been designated as described in Section M.3.

Drainage Area 7

Water within the Glass Sorting Area and the Commingled Container Storage Area is contained
with berms, sumps, and holding tanks. A valley trench (GSA-VG) is located in front of the Glass
Sorting area which directs water towards Sump GSA-VGS. A valley trench is also located in
front of the Commingled Container Storage area (CCS-VG) which directs water towards Sump
CCS-VGS. These sumps have a high liquid level float switch. When the float switch detects a

                                                                                               10
high liquid level, pumps are turned on and flow is pumped to two, 4,000-gallon interconnected
tanks. A third tank, with a volume of 5,400 gallons, is located next to the existing tanks but is
not connected to them. If the water level in the interconnected tanks is high, stormwater from
one of those tanks is pumped into the third tank for additional storage. Water within the tanks
is discharged to EBMUD sanitary sewer after 24 hours of dry weather under permit via a 4-inch
pipe with a flow meter and ball valve. Water from within the Commingled Container Storage
area may overtop the berm and flow into Drainage Area 5 towards discharge point DP-5A.
Additional tanks may be brought in as-needed in advance of heavy rain events to provide
additional storage.

When the liquid in the stormwater holding tanks rises to a high level, the float switch sensors
send an electrical signal that turn off the sump pumps. The pumps remain deactivated until the
liquid drops back down to a low level. During large storm events that exceed the tank storage
capacity, water within the Glass Sorting Area may overtop the berm and flow into Drainage
Area 9 towards discharge point DP-9 as described in Section M.3.

Drainage Area 8

This Drainage Area contains operations by the Recycling Center including industrial activities
from the Customer Recyclable and Recyclable Buyback Areas and a portion of the Paper
Recycling Warehouse. Non-industrial activities within this Drainage Area include the Employee
Parking and lunch area. DP-8A is a catch basin that is connected to the City’s stormwater
conveyance system on Gilman Street. Stormwater is collected as it enters the catch basin.

Drainage Area 9

This Drainage Area includes a portion of the Container Bin Storage Area, the eastern portion of
the Glass Recycling Warehouse, and the eastern portion of the Paper Recycling Warehouse.
Stormwater from this Drainage Area flows down the eastern alley of the Paper Recycling
Warehouse and discharges as sheet flow to RSR sampling point DP-9 towards Gilman Street as
described in Section M.3. Water from within the Glass Sorting Area may overtop the berm and
flow into Drainage Area 9 towards discharge point DP-9 during large storm events. During
large storm events, run-on from the off-site adjacent railroad can overtop the curb located
along the eastern boundary of the Drainage Area and can comingle with on-site industrial
water, Figure 3.
                                                                                                    11
Drainage Area 10

This Drainage Area contains the Transfer Station building, Construction Debris,
General/Electronic Waste Storage and Garbage Truck Parking areas. Within the Transfer Station
building is a Vactor Truck wash area. Customers bring their materials for disposal in this
Drainage Area.

Flow in Drainage Area 10 is routed to trench drains in front of the Construction Debris
receiving area (TD-4) and near the General/Electronic Waste Storage Area (TD-3) (Figure 3).

TD-4 directs flow to a manhole with two sluice gates. The sluice gate directing flow to the
stormwater conveyance system (gate closest to TD-4) is maintained in the open position while
the sanitary sewer sluice gate is maintained in the closed position. Flow is directed to the main
stormwater conveyance system, where it is joined by flow from trench drain TD-3. Flow
proceeds via gravity flow to a second manhole equipped with a weir to deflect flow from going
toward catch basin CB-1. Flow is instead directed to the stormwater holding tank(s) via a 2-
inch pipe inlet by gravity flow. The stormwater holding tank is a 21,000-gallon aboveground
storage tank. At least 24-hours after a rain event, the Environmental Compliance Specialist
drains the 21,000-gallon tank to a sump pump with a digital flowmeter that pumps water to
the Sanitary Sewer System. A second 21,000-gallon tank is present for additional storage, but
is not directly plumbed to the stormwater system. Additional tanks are brought on-site for
larger events to prevent discharge. Stormwater within the tank(s) is discharged into East Bay
Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) sanitary sewer after 24 hours of dry weather under permit.
During high flow events, stormwater that bypasses the weir flows to the municipal stormwater
system and is sampled at location DP-1A after passing through a Contech filter vault.

The Vactor Truck wash area, located inside the Transfer Station Building, is bermed and has a
trench drain. Wash water flows into the trench drain to the sanitary sewer (Figure 3). Behind
the Vactor Truck wash area wall, an additional trench drain exists that connects to the same
sanitary sewer line.

Drainage Area 11 – Non-Industrial

Drainage Area 11 is non-industrial and includes the western portion of the Green Waste
Receiving Area roof that discharges to landscaped areas and Second Street.

                                                                                                12
C.4       NEIGHBORING OPERATIONS AND STORMWATER RUN-ON
C.4.1       Neighboring Operations and Run-On

North: To the north of the Facility is Codornices Creek. There have been no recorded incidents
of the creek flooding into Drainage Area 1. The northern area of Second Street is adjacent to
the Facility and may flood with municipal stormwater during extreme rain events. When
flooding occurs, it may impede the flow Facility drainage to the municipal storm drain system,
but no overland run-on to the Facility has been recorded.

South: To the south of the Facility is Gilman Street. There is no potential run-on from this area
as Gilman Street is at a lower elevation than the Facility.

East: To the east of the Facility are railroad tracks. There is run-on from this area during large
storm events to Drainage Area 9.

West: To the west of the Facility is Second Street. This street floods during large back to back
storm events, which can impede Facility drainage to the municipal storm drain system, but no
overland run-on to the Facility has been recorded.
